accuracy.evidence: Checked against the KS3 science programme of study for England (magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; fields plotted with a compass and shown by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation), NGSS MS-PS2-5, IOP Supporting Physics Teaching 11-14 on magnetism, and BGS/NOAA geomagnetism pages (field roughly a tilted bar magnet about 10° off the spin axis; the Arctic magnetic pole attracts the north-seeking end, so it is a south-type pole; magnetic north drifts yearly). Field-line convention (direction of a compass N end, N to S outside) and the line-density reading of strength are stated as conventions. The lab's lines come from a two-point-pole 1/r² model, named as a model in the adult text; spot strengths were checked numerically (pole P 100%, middle Q 25%, far R 5%). The Earth scene shows only the horizontal component at the surface, as a flat compass does, and the adult text notes the dip. Declination items follow the standard rule (east: subtract; west: add).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented KS3 magnetism misconceptions (IOP SPT, AAAS/Driver et al. on magnetism): lines drawn S to N (quiz 'dir', p1); field strongest beside the middle (scene 2 prediction and Q-first refusal, quiz 'middle', m2); field the same everywhere ('same'); lines crossing or joining between like poles (scene 3 prediction, myth card, m3, m8); a compass near a magnet still points to geographic north (scene 1 prediction 'Towards the magnet's N pole', quiz 'earth' and 'attractN'); the Arctic pole as a north magnetic pole (scene 4 prediction and N-top refusal, quiz 'earthN', p5); field stops at the magnet's edge or lies only in a flat plane (myth cards, m9); a compass points exactly at the North Pole (myth card 'exact').

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built on this topic's own mechanism: a draggable plotting compass whose needle follows a computed field and leaves arrows until traced field lines appear; spots ranked by field strength with live meters; a second magnet flipped between attract and repel patterns with a probe that finds the neutral point; an inner Earth magnet flipped until flat compasses in three places point to the Arctic. The lab-distinct gate passes under 30% against every flagship, including flagpoles (608 Magnetic Poles), flagefield (electric fields) and flagglobe; none plots a field with a compass, finds a neutral point or models the Earth's dipole.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is discovered before it is stated: plotting six compass arrows makes the N-to-S loops appear; the strength meters show P 100%, Q 25%, R 5% only after the learner ranks them, and a Q-first tap is refused with a reason; flipping magnet B shows the lines join across for N-S and turn away for N-N, and only the midway probe in the repel case reads 'no field'; compasses in Canada, at the equator and in New Zealand point to Antarctica until the Earth's magnet is flipped S-up. The done messages then name each rule.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Towards the magnet's N pole' (the needle swings away from N); 'Beside the middle of the magnet' (the meters put the pole first); 'Join straight across the gap' for two N poles (lines turn away and a neutral point appears); 'A north pole' in the Arctic (with N up, every compass points to Antarctica).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; each wrong option maps to its own slip message in slip(): 'dir' (backwards direction), 'straight' (lines do not curve), 'middle' and 'same' (strength and spacing), 'attractN' and 'earth' (compass near a magnet), 'cancel'/'cross' (one direction at each place), 'earthN' and 'star' (why a compass points north), 'strong' (neutral point between like poles), 'broken'/'off' (steel changes the local field).

readability.evidence: Kid text FK grade 3.5 and adult text 9.2 by learn/readability.py (limits 6.5 and 9.5 for a learner lesson). Kid paragraphs use the KS3 terms the topic needs (magnetic field, plotting compass, field lines, poles, neutral point, attract, repel) with one idea per sentence; canvas prompts are short, such as 'Where is the field strongest?' and 'Why does a compass point north?'.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph teaches one idea (what a field is and how to map it; line direction and spacing; two-magnet patterns; the Earth's field); the adult text gives curriculum placement, the line convention and the model used, the Earth facts with the flat-compass caveat, named mistakes, and what the lab does. The content gate finds no filler and the explanation is under 12% similar to every other lesson, including 608 Magnetic Poles and 1047 Electric fields.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 390 px screenshots of all six steps (mid-task and finished) and a 1200 px dark-theme set: the magnet, field lines, compasses and labels are readable; labels over field lines have a white backing; the 8 fact cards fit in a 2 by 4 grid with wrapped text. Real pointer drags on a 390 px viewport plotted compass arrows (including a refusal on the magnet), ranked spots, flipped magnet B, found the neutral point, flipped the Earth's magnet, checked Canada, and dragged cards into True and Myth, each with the expected spoken feedback.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label (move compass to the next spot, plot an arrow here, 'Spot P is next strongest', flip magnet B, test midway, flip the Earth's magnet, check each place, True/Myth for each card). The canvas aria-label carries each spoken result, such as 'Arrow 2 plotted beside the middle: the needle points left'. The pipeline walkthrough completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, showed the challenge, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme, with no console errors.
